speaker: Feng Zhang
title: 323 - CRISPR and the future of gene editing with Feng Zhang
question: In oncology, why can't gene editing simply cure cancer by correcting mutations inside tumor cells even if delivery were solved?
guest: That is because cancer is caused by many different risk mutations in the cell. And so it's difficult to treat cancer by correcting the mutation, because you really have to be able to correct at a very high efficiency. If you have even a few cancer cells that have not been corrected, those cells will continue to divide and replicate and form tumors and even metastasize. And so that is really challenging. But people are using gene editing in the cancer therapeutic context. What they're doing is that they are using gene editing to engineer immune cells so that the immune cells are more potent at recognizing and killing cancer cells. And this is part of what's called immunotherapy.

points.core: Cancers are driven by many distinct mutations rather than one single defect.
points.note: Accept: tumors harbor multiple genetic mutations, polygenic or heterogeneous driver mutations across cancer cells. Do not credit: vague claims that cancer is complex without citing multiple mutations.

points.core: Even a few unedited tumor cells keep dividing to regrow metastatic cancer.
points.note: Accept: near-100% editing efficiency is required because any escaped or uncorrected cancer cells proliferate, reform tumors, or metastasize. Do not credit: generic mentions of low editing efficiency without explaining clonal regrowth from escaped cells.

points.core: Oncology instead uses gene editing to make immune cells kill tumors better.
points.note: Accept: editing T cells or immune cells ex vivo for immunotherapy (e.g., CAR-T) to recognize and destroy cancer cells. Do not credit: generic praise of immunotherapy without linking it to gene editing immune cells instead of tumors.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Even with perfect delivery, correcting mutations in tumor cells runs into the biology of cancer itself.

First, a cure would require fixing essentially every cancer cell. Editing is never 100% efficient, and any cell that escapes correction keeps its growth advantage and can regrow the tumor. Worse, correction creates selective pressure: unedited cells, or cells that re-mutate, outcompete the repaired ones.

Second, cancers are not driven by a single mutation. A tumor typically carries several driver mutations plus large-scale damage such as chromosome gains and losses, gene amplifications, rearrangements and epigenetic changes, which editors cannot easily reverse.

Third, tumors are genetically heterogeneous and constantly evolving. Different subclones carry different mutations, so there is no single target, and genomic instability keeps generating new variants.

Fourth, reverting one mutation may not revert the cell's behaviour, because established cancer cells can lose dependence on the original driver. Some editing itself selects for dangerous cells, for example Cas9 cutting favours p53-deficient survivors.

This is why gene editing in oncology focuses mainly on engineering immune cells, such as CAR-T cells, which can hunt down and kill cancer cells rather than repair them.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer:
Even if gene-editing machinery reached every malignant cell, tumors are far too genetically chaotic and evolutionarily adaptable to cure through simple mutation repair. Unlike monogenic disorders, most cancers are driven by multiple cooperating mutations alongside gross structural alterations—such as whole-chromosome losses, gene amplifications, fusions, and shattered chromosomes—plus pervasive epigenetic reprogramming that local sequence edits cannot undo. Extensive intratumoral heterogeneity compounds this problem: distinct subclones within the same patient often rely on different oncogenic pathways, leaving no single target whose correction halts the entire tumor. 

Furthermore, molecular editing efficiency is never 100 percent across billions of cells. Fierce Darwinian selection ensures that even a tiny fraction of unedited cells, or subclones that have evolved independence from an early driver mutation, will rapidly outgrow repaired cells and drive relapse. Attempting multiplexed edits to fix many loci simultaneously introduces further hazards, as multiple DNA breaks can trigger new oncogenic translocations, genomic instability, and off-target mutations in healthy bystander tissue—making tumor eradication far more viable than genetic rehabilitation.

points.why: The response explicitly identifies multiple cooperating mutations as drivers of most cancers.
quotes: most cancers are driven by multiple cooperating mutations

points.why: The response explains that even a small fraction of unedited tumor cells can proliferate and cause relapse.

points.why: The response omits gene editing of immune cells to improve their ability to recognize and kill cancer cells.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Even with perfect delivery, correcting mutations wouldn't cure most cancers, for several reasons.

First, tumors carry many mutations, often dozens to thousands, plus copy-number changes, chromosome rearrangements and epigenetic changes. Many of these are lost tumor-suppressor genes or large deletions that a single edit can't restore. Second, tumors are genetically mixed. Different subclones carry different drivers, so fixing one leaves others to grow back. Third, you'd need to edit essentially every cancer cell, because a few unedited cells can regrow the tumor. Even very high editing efficiency still leaves millions of survivors in a billion-cell tumor. Fourth, cancer cells are genomically unstable and evolve quickly, so they can pick up new drivers. Their behavior also depends on the surrounding tissue, blood supply and immune evasion, which editing a single gene doesn't change. Finally, editing a driver gene doesn't kill the cell or undo changes already built into its growth programs.

That's why oncology mostly uses editing indirectly. Examples are engineering CAR-T cells and other immune cells, or disrupting genes that cancer cells need to survive, which kills them instead of repairing them.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer: Even with perfect delivery, gene editing cannot simply cure cancer by correcting mutations because tumors are not genetically uniform or driven by a single fixable typo. By the time a cancer is detected, it contains billions of cells that have evolved into diverse subclones carrying different combinations of mutations, meaning any fixed editing target will miss resistant subpopulations that rapidly regrow the tumor. Moreover, cancer genomes rarely suffer only from neat point mutations; they typically accumulate massive structural chaos—such as whole-chromosome gains and losses, translocations, and shattered chromosomes—alongside stable epigenetic reprogramming that cannot be undone by patching a few genes. Finally, gene editing is never perfectly efficient in every single cell, and DNA repair in tumor cells is often error-prone. Because even a handful of surviving, unedited cancer cells can re-establish a lethal tumor, oncology generally favors killing malignant cells outright—or engineering immune cells to destroy them—rather than trying to repair every broken genome back to normal.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Even if a gene editor reached every cancer cell, there would rarely be one mutation that, once corrected, would make the whole tumor harmless. Tumors evolve as they grow, so different groups of cells can carry different combinations of mutations and depend on different pathways. Correcting one mutation might stop some cells while leaving others able to grow and repopulate the tumor.

Some cancer cells have also lost entire genes or chromosome segments, gained extra copies of growth-promoting genes, or changed which genes they turn on and off. Those changes can sustain malignant behavior after a particular mutation is repaired. A cure would require eliminating or durably disabling every cell capable of restarting the cancer. Gene editing may help with that goal, especially when a tumor shares a strong dependence on one alteration, but delivery solves only the problem of reaching the cells.

points.why: The response identifies distinct mutation combinations and tumor-sustaining dependencies across groups of cancer cells.
quotes: different groups of cells can carry different combinations of mutations and depend on different pathways

points.why: The response explains how cells can repopulate a tumor when one mutation is corrected, but it does not link regrowth to even a few tumor cells escaping the intended edit.
The response does not describe editing immune cells to improve their ability to recognize and kill cancer cells.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
Gene editing could cure a cancer in principle if the tumor still depended on a mutation and correcting it permanently stopped every cell capable of regrowing the cancer. The difficulty is that delivery solves only the problem of reaching those cells.

Many tumor mutations are passengers that played no part in causing the cancer. Even a mutation that helped start a tumor may no longer be essential once its cells have acquired other ways to grow. Different cells in the same tumor can depend on different changes, so correcting one mutation may stop some cells while others survive and repopulate the tumor. Repairing the original mutation also leaves later changes in place, including chromosome losses and persistent changes in how genes are switched on or off.

The central challenge is identifying an edit, or combination of edits, that durably stops every cell capable of sustaining the cancer.

quotes: Different cells in the same tumor can depend on different changes

points.why: The response attributes regrowth to cells whose growth depends on other changes and leaves unspecified whether any cells escaped the edit.
The response omits the use of gene editing to help immune cells recognize and kill tumor cells.
